name: Umar Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Umar. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on patrol on the south side, which is the Foundry Road industrial estate and the Millbrook estate next to it. Break-ins at the warehouses at night, catalytic converters stolen off vans, a lot of fly-tipping, and sometimes a fight at the snooker hall. I'm two years in. I failed my first police driving course, so for now I'm mostly the passenger or on foot, which is a bit embarrassing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the business owners. They know me, they call me first, and when I get their stolen van back they shake my hand like I'm family. Hard is the night shifts and the waiting, hours of sitting in a car watching a gate. The force gave us a translation tool on our phones last year, and I use it now and then with the lorry drivers, once I saw the others using it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and rent a room in a shared house on Brook Street, five minutes from my parents. On my days off I help my dad at his tyre shop on Foundry Road. Last year I co-signed a loan for a new tyre-changing machine for the shop, and I pay part of it. So I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. Okay. My dad will say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a reminder that real work is done by people who turn up. At work I'd say keep the money for more officers on nights. I don't post much, maybe something in the family group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, my job is fine. What I worry about is the shop. The big tyre chain on the ring road is taking customers with cheap online booking, and if Dad's shop struggles, I'm paying more of that loan. So nothing changes, but nothing gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retake the police driving course in the spring, so I'm not stuck as a passenger. I'd keep helping at the shop on days off, maybe set up a simple booking page so people can book tyres online like at the big chain. And I'd put a little aside every month, even fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit tired, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set up a booking page. Would you use AI for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if my cousin shows me how. My cousin Nadia did one for her nail salon with one of those tools in an afternoon. I'm not going to be the first to try things, but I'm not stupid either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if the shop goes under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the loan is mine, about four thousand left. I'd have to pay it off from my police pay over two or three years. My dad would be devastated, more than me. That shop is his life.

say: Real work is done by **people who turn up**.
Keep the money for **more officers** on nights.
I'd share it in the **family group chat**, not much online.
think: My job is fine; I worry about **Dad's tyre shop** against the big chain.
If the shop struggles, I pay more of the **co-signed loan**.
do: Retake the **police driving course** in spring.
Set up an **online booking page** for the tyre shop.
S0.quote: I'm not going to be the first to try things, but I'm not stupid either.
fieldNote: His money risk runs through **his father's shop** and a loan he co-signed.
Steady with tech: he'll try things **once family shows him**.
Embarrassed about **failing the driving course**, which he wants to fix.

steps.text: Retake the police driving course in the spring
Set up an online tyre booking page for his dad's shop
Save fifty a month toward the shop loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like where it's heading. The forms first, then the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to let computers do the forms if it puts more officers out at night. Fewer forms, more patrols, that's a good trade. At the station I'd say it, and to the business owners on Foundry Road too, because they want to see us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's mostly fine for me. My job is out on the estate, watching gates and talking to people, and that's not what the card says goes first. The bigger change is at the shop, because the big chain will use AI for booking and pricing and Dad will look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the new tools training once the others have done it and say it works. I'd help Dad with an AI booking and reminder system for the shop, so he keeps up. And I'd keep paying the loan and saving a bit each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's a change, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad accept an AI booking system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would grumble for a week and then love it, same as he did with the card machine. The trick is to set it up and show him it works, not ask first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the station would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room staff, the ones answering 999 calls and sending cars. That's a lot of what the card says: answering and planning. My cousin's husband works there, and he's got three kids.

say: Let computers do the **forms** if it puts more officers out at night.
**Fewer forms, more patrols**: that's a good trade.
think: My work is **out on the estate**, which isn't what goes first.
The bigger change is the **shop**, where the big chain will look faster.
do: Take **tools training** once others say it works.
Set up an **AI booking and reminder** system for the shop.

fieldNote: He sees his **patrol work** as fairly safe from early AI.
Uses AI to help **the family business** keep up with chains.
Shows **steady** pattern: waits for proof from others.

steps.text: Take the force's tools training after colleagues test it
Install an AI booking and reminder system at the tyre shop
Keep up loan payments and save a little each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the faster ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. Two years. That's a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government shouldn't rush, but I'd also say families and businesses need to be ready, not wait for help. At work I'd say police are still needed on the ground. At the mosque I'd say we should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the force gets smaller, with all the reports, calls and planning done by machines by 2028. Patrol lasts a bit longer, until the robots around 2031. I'm junior and not the strongest, so I could be cut. But I have the shop, and changing tyres is hands-on, so that buys me some years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start learning the shop side properly: the ordering, the suppliers, the accounts, so I could run it if I had to. I'd stay in the police as long as they'd keep me and save hard. And I'd talk to Dad about taking the shop over in a few years, maybe bringing my cousin in too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I have something to fall back on. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said changing tyres buys you years. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure, no. Robots will come for tyres eventually, the card says around 2031. But people will still bring their van to a man they trust for a while after the robots come. I'd bet on that more than on a police job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be pleased I'm near the family business. My dad would be quietly happy, and then he'd start telling me how to do everything. That's the price.

say: Families and businesses should **be ready**, not wait for help.
At the mosque I'd say we should **look after each other**.
think: The force gets **smaller**, and as a junior I could be cut.
Changing tyres is **hands-on**, so the shop buys me some years.
do: Learn the shop's **ordering, suppliers and accounts**.
Stay in the police as long as possible and **save hard**.
Talk to his dad about **taking over** the shop with his cousin.
feel: **Anxious**, but comforted by a family fallback.
S2.quote: People will still bring their van to a man they trust for a while after the robots come.
fieldNote: His **family business** is a real fallback that reduces panic.
He sees the **three-year gap** as protecting hands-on trade work.
Traditional view: **self-reliance** and community support over government.

steps.text: Save as much as possible while still in the police
Plan to take over his dad's tyre shop on Foundry Road
Bring his cousin into the tyre shop to share the work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. That's more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to prepare, so let's prepare instead of complain. At the station I'd tell the young ones to have a backup. I'd say the same at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I can stay a police officer and build up the shop on the side. By 2031 the shop would have a booking system and loyal customers. When the police side shrinks, I'd step across, and the hands-on work lasts till about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pass the driving course and keep doing my police job well. I'd buy a second-hand wheel alignment machine for the shop with Dad, maybe two thousand, so we can offer more. And I'd learn the AI tools at work once others are using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. A bit of worry, but I can see a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand for a machine with two weeks of savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spread over a year with a small loan, and the shop would pay it back with alignment jobs. It's a risk, but a careful one. Dad's done the numbers with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be a police officer if you didn't have to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I like it, especially the business owners. If the police kept me, I'd stay and help Dad on weekends. The tyre shop is the backup, not the dream.

say: We have **time to prepare**, so let's prepare instead of complain.
I'd say the same at the **mosque**, to the families there.
think: Five years lets me stay in the police and **build the shop** on the side.
When the police side shrinks, I'd **step across** to the shop.
do: Pass the **driving course** and keep doing the police job well.
Buy a second-hand **alignment machine** for about two thousand.
Learn work **AI tools** once others use them.
feel: **Fairly okay**, with some worry but a clear road.
S3.quote: The tyre shop is the backup, not the dream.
fieldNote: With five years he builds a **two-track life**: police and family shop.
Willing to take a **careful risk** on new equipment.
Still likes policing; the shop is **insurance**.

steps.text: Pass the police driving course and stay on patrol
Buy a second-hand wheel alignment machine for the shop
Learn the force AI tools once colleagues use them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time to plan, so no excuses. At work I'd say the same. In the community I'd say teach the kids a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels safe for me. I'd have a decade in the police and the shop growing on the side. Money is tight now, but in ten years the loan's long gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as normal, pass the driving course, learn the tools when they come. I'd keep helping at the shop and save a little more once the loan is paid. Maybe I'd think about marrying and settling down too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Not much to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does 2039, when robots arrive, worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. By then I'd be forty. But I'd have savings, a trade, and a shop. That's more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young cousin starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade with your hands, and learn the computers too. Don't rely on one thing. My dad taught me that with the shop.

say: There's **plenty of time** to plan, so no excuses.
In the community I'd say **teach the kids** a trade.
think: Ten years feels **safe**, with police work and the shop growing.
The **loan** will be long gone by then.
do: Pass the **driving course** and learn tools when they come.
Keep helping at the **shop** and save more after the loan.
S4.quote: Get a trade with your hands, and learn the computers too.
fieldNote: With a decade, he feels **secure** but money is still thin today.
He values **trades plus computers**, a blended approach.
Family advice from **his father** guides his outlook.

steps.text: Keep patrolling Foundry Road and pass the driving course
Save more once the shop loan is paid off

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to set up the shop properly or pay off the loan. What would help is apprenticeships and small business help, like cheap loans for family firms, not handouts. And the police keeping juniors on long enough to plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people I serve. The businesses on Foundry Road call me because they know me. If they get a machine instead, they'll stop calling.

headlineQuote: The businesses on Foundry Road call me because they know me. If they get a machine instead, they'll stop calling.
portrait: A **27-year-old patrol constable** on the industrial south side, still a passenger after failing the driving course.
Single, renting a room near his parents, and **co-signer** on a loan for his dad's tyre shop.
Uses AI tools **once others have**, and wants to help the shop keep up with chains.
Sees the **family tyre shop** as his backup, softening even the fastest scenarios.
Believes in **work, trades and family** over government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to set up the shop or clear the loan.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** and cheap loans for family firms, not handouts.
The force keeping **juniors** on long enough to plan.
